# Tool notes
Reference slides for reading after the talk

## pixi / uv

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="42%" .compact}
[Must have]{.accent-strong}

Project environment managers: dependencies declared in one file, exact versions pinned in a **lockfile** committed to git.

**For the agent:** one command gives a working environment, and the same command runs the tests.
No guessing which Python or which `pip install`.

**For you:** the agent, you and CI run identical versions. No "works on my machine".

**Which one:** pixi when you need conda-forge (compilers, CUDA, non-Python libraries);
uv for pure-Python projects.

[pixi.sh](https://pixi.sh) · [docs.astral.sh/uv](https://docs.astral.sh/uv)
:::

::: {.column width="58%"}
```bash
# pixi: conda-forge + PyPI, writes pixi.toml + pixi.lock
pixi init
pixi add python=3.13 numpy pytest
pixi add --pypi jaxtyping
pixi task add test "pytest -q"
pixi run test
```

```bash
# uv: PyPI only, writes pyproject.toml + uv.lock
uv init --lib
uv add numpy
uv add --dev pytest
uv run pytest -q
```

```bash
# CI: install exactly what the lockfile says
pixi install --locked          # or: uv sync --locked
```
:::
::::

::: notes
Telling the agent "run tests with pixi run test" (or uv run pytest) in CLAUDE.md removes a whole
class of environment confusion: the command builds or reuses the right environment first.
pixi tasks double as documentation of how the project is meant to be run.
This deck itself uses pixi for its preview and render tasks.
:::

## pytest

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="42%" .compact}
[Must have]{.accent-strong}

The standard Python test runner: plain `assert`, fixtures, parametrized tests.

**For the agent:** a pass/fail signal after every change. The spec, made executable.

**For you:** tests are the reviewable form of the spec. Read them *before* the code exists.

**Wire it in:** tell the agent to run `pytest` before it reports a task done (`CLAUDE.md`), and run it in CI.

[docs.pytest.org](https://docs.pytest.org)
:::

::: {.column width="58%"}
```python
def kinetic_energy(mass, velocity):
    return 0.5 * mass * velocity**2
```

```python
import pytest


def test_kinetic_energy():
    assert kinetic_energy(2.0, 3.0) == pytest.approx(9.0)


@pytest.mark.parametrize("velocity", [-3.0, 3.0])
def test_direction_does_not_matter(velocity):
    assert kinetic_energy(2.0, velocity) == pytest.approx(9.0)
```

```text
$ pytest -q
..                                                       [100%]
2 passed
```
:::
::::

::: notes
All code on these tool slides was run with current versions of each tool;
the outputs shown are real.
:::

## ruff

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="42%" .compact}
[Too cheap to skip]{.accent-strong}

A very fast linter and formatter. It replaces flake8, isort, black and friends.

**For the agent:** immediate feedback on common mistakes; `--fix` repairs many of them.

**For you:** consistent formatting means a diff shows only real changes, so review
is about the logic, not the style.

[docs.astral.sh/ruff](https://docs.astral.sh/ruff)
:::

::: {.column width="58%"}
```python
import os


def collect(value, results=[]):
    results.append(value)
    return results
```

```text
$ ruff check
messy.py:1:8: F401 [*] `os` imported but unused
messy.py:4:28: B006 Do not use mutable data structures
                    for argument defaults
```

```toml
# pyproject.toml
[tool.ruff.lint]
select = ["E", "F", "I", "B", "UP"]
```
:::
::::

::: notes
B006 is a real bug, not style: the default list is created once and shared between
calls, so results from one call leak into the next.
The rule selection is a matter of taste; B (bugbear) is the one most likely to catch real bugs.
:::

## mypy

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="42%" .compact}
[Too cheap to skip]{.accent-strong}

A static type checker for annotated Python.

**For the agent:** catches interface mismatches before anything runs: wrong argument
types, a forgotten `None`.

**For you:** type signatures document the interfaces, and a typed function is quicker to review.

**Limits:** it doesn't see array shapes (see jaxtyping).

[mypy.readthedocs.io](https://mypy.readthedocs.io)
:::

::: {.column width="58%"}
```python
def find_index(items: list[str], target: str) -> int | None:
    for i, item in enumerate(items):
        if item == target:
            return i
    return None


def next_index(items: list[str], target: str) -> int:
    return find_index(items, target) + 1
```

```text
$ mypy lookup.py
lookup.py:9: error: Unsupported operand types for +
                    ("None" and "int")
```
:::
::::

::: notes
Without mypy, this only fails at run time, and only when the target is missing.
Config used: [tool.mypy] strict = true.
:::

## Quarto

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="42%" .compact}
[High value for scientific code]{.accent-strong}

A publishing system that runs code inside documents: websites, reports, slides (this deck).

**For the agent:** a place to write the spec down and to run the code on a real problem.
A broken validation shows up as a failed render.

**For you:** prose, code and results in one place you can *read*. Versioned with the code,
shared between sessions.

**Wire it in:** render in CI, so the validation documents run on every push.

[quarto.org](https://quarto.org)
:::

::: {.column width="58%"}
````markdown
---
title: "Validation: numerical derivative"
---

The finite-difference derivative of sin(x)
should match cos(x).

```{{python}}
x = np.linspace(0, 2 * np.pi, 200)
dydx = np.gradient(np.sin(x), x)
print(f"max error: {np.max(np.abs(dydx - np.cos(x))):.1e}")

plt.plot(x, np.cos(x), label="analytic")
plt.plot(x, dydx, "--", label="numerical")
plt.legend()
```
````

[Renders to a page with the text, the plot, and `max error: 1.7e-04`.]{.muted .compact}
:::
::::

::: notes
For expensive validation documents, Quarto's freeze option avoids re-running them on
every render, at the cost of them no longer running in CI.
:::

## hypothesis

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="42%" .compact}
[High value for scientific code]{.accent-strong}

Property-based testing: you state a property, hypothesis generates many inputs, and shrinks any failure to a minimal example.

**For the agent:** it can't pass by getting a few hand-picked cases right.

**For you:** invariants written once: round-trips, conservation, symmetry, bounds.

[hypothesis.readthedocs.io](https://hypothesis.readthedocs.io)
:::

::: {.column width="58%"}
```python
HARTREE_IN_EV = 27.211386245988

def ev_to_hartree(e):
    return e / HARTREE_IN_EV

def hartree_to_ev(e):
    return e * HARTREE_IN_EV
```

```python
from hypothesis import given
from hypothesis import strategies as st


@given(st.floats(min_value=-1e6, max_value=1e6))
def test_roundtrip(energy):
    roundtrip = hartree_to_ev(ev_to_hartree(energy))
    assert roundtrip == pytest.approx(energy)
```

[One test, run on 100 generated energies by default.]{.muted .compact}
:::
::::

::: notes
With JAX, every new array shape triggers a recompile under jit, so keep shapes fixed and
let hypothesis vary the values.
:::

## jaxtyping

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="42%" .compact}
[When you need more confidence]{.accent-strong}

Shape and dtype annotations for JAX, NumPy and PyTorch arrays, checked at runtime (here with beartype).

**For the agent:** a shape mismatch fails loudly at the function boundary,
instead of silently broadcasting.

**For you:** signatures say what each axis means.

**Check in tests only:** annotate without a decorator, and let the pytest hook switch
checking on. Normal imports stay unchecked, so production code pays nothing.

[docs.kidger.site/jaxtyping](https://docs.kidger.site/jaxtyping)
:::

::: {.column width="58%"}
```python
def weighted_sum(
    w: Float[Array, " n"], x: Float[Array, " n"]
) -> Float[Array, ""]:
    return jnp.sum(w * x)

w = jnp.array([1.0, 2.0, 3.0])
x = jnp.ones((3, 1))    # oops: column, not vector
weighted_sum(w, x)      # 18.0, should be 6.0: unchecked
```

```text
$ pytest --jaxtyping-packages=mypkg,beartype.beartype
E  jaxtyping.TypeCheckError: Type-check error whilst
   checking the parameters of mypkg.weighted_sum.
```

```toml
# pyproject.toml: make it the default for every test run
[tool.pytest.ini_options]
addopts = "--jaxtyping-packages=mypkg,beartype.beartype"
```
:::
::::

::: notes
Without the hook, the annotations are inert: the (3,) * (3, 1) product broadcasts to a
(3, 3) array and sums all nine entries. No error, wrong answer.
Outside pytest, the same hook is available as jaxtyping.install_import_hook, or per
function with the @jaxtyped(typechecker=beartype) decorator.
Under jax.jit the checks run at trace time, so even when enabled they cost little.
Tested with jaxtyping 0.3.11 on Python 3.13; the import hook failed on Python 3.15 at the time of writing.
:::

## mutmut

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="42%" .compact}
[When you need more confidence]{.accent-strong}

Mutation testing: makes small changes to your code (flip `<=` to `<`, change a constant) and checks whether any test notices.

**For you:** can the tests actually fail? A surviving mutant is a change no test catches.

Not every survivor is a bug, so read them.

**Cost:** runs the test suite once per mutant, so run it now and then, not on every commit.

[github.com/boxed/mutmut](https://github.com/boxed/mutmut)
:::

::: {.column width="58%"}
```python
def is_converged(error, tol):
    return error <= tol

def test_is_converged():
    assert is_converged(1e-8, tol=1e-6)
    assert not is_converged(1e-3, tol=1e-6)
```

```text
$ mutmut run && mutmut results
is_converged__mutmut_1: survived
-    return error <= tol
+    return error < tol
```

```python
def test_is_converged_at_tolerance():   # kills the mutant
    assert is_converged(1e-6, tol=1e-6)
```
:::
::::

::: notes
Configure which code to mutate in pyproject.toml: [tool.mutmut] source_paths = ["src/yourpkg/"].
(Older versions call it paths_to_mutate.)
Survivors that change nothing observable are "equivalent mutants" and can be ignored.
:::
